name: Force of Nature
subject: Weather, oceans, volcanoes and earthquakes
tagline: Twenty questions on storms, waves, eruptions and the restless planet under your feet. Starts easy, ends hard.

questions.q: What is the name for the calm, clear centre of a hurricane?
questions.w: The eye, typically 30 to 65 kilometres across, where air sinks and skies can be blue.
questions.more: The strongest winds blow in the eyewall around it. People caught in the eye have been fooled into thinking the storm was over, only to be hit from the other direction. Hurricane-hunter aircraft fly straight through the eyewall into the eye to measure the pressure, the best gauge of a storm's strength.

questions.q: On which scale, from 0 to 5, are hurricanes rated by wind speed?
questions.w: The Saffir-Simpson scale, devised in 1971 by an engineer and a meteorologist in Florida.
questions.more: A Category 5 has sustained winds above 157 miles per hour. The Beaufort scale rates wind from 0 to 12 by its effect on the sea, the Fujita scale rates tornadoes by damage, and Richter is for earthquakes. Atlantic storms are named from six alphabetical lists that repeat every six years; the deadliest names are retired.

questions.q: What is the hottest layer of the Earth, at its very centre?
questions.w: The inner core, a ball of solid iron and nickel about as hot as the surface of the Sun, around 5,400 degrees Celsius.
questions.more: It stays solid despite the heat because of the crushing pressure. The liquid outer core around it churns and generates the magnetic field that steers compasses and shields us from solar wind. The deepest hole humans have ever drilled, in Russia, reached only 12 kilometres, a third of the way through the crust.

questions.q: Which is the largest ocean on Earth?
questions.w: The Pacific, which covers about a third of the planet's surface and holds more than half its free water.
questions.more: It is bigger than all the land on Earth put together. Magellan named it Mar Pacífico, the peaceful sea, in 1520 after a calm crossing, which is not how most sailors have found it. Its deepest point, the Challenger Deep, is nearly 11 kilometres down; Everest would fit inside with two kilometres to spare.

questions.q: What do we call a giant sea wave set off by an undersea earthquake or landslide?
questions.w: A tsunami, from the Japanese for 'harbour wave'.
questions.more: In the open ocean a tsunami may be less than a metre high and pass under ships unnoticed, travelling at the speed of a jet airliner. It rears up only as it reaches shallow water. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed around 230,000 people in fourteen countries; the sea pulling far out from the beach is the warning sign.

questions.q: The eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79 buried which Roman town under ash?
questions.w: Pompeii, along with its neighbour Herculaneum, which was swamped by a flow of superheated gas and rock.
questions.more: Pliny the Younger watched from across the bay and described a cloud shaped like an umbrella pine; eruptions of that type are still called Plinian. The towns were lost for 1,500 years. The famous plaster casts of victims were made in the 1860s by pouring plaster into the hollows their bodies left in the ash. Three million people live near Vesuvius today.

questions.q: The Ring of Fire, where about three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes sit, circles which ocean?
questions.w: The Pacific, along a 40,000-kilometre horseshoe from New Zealand up through Japan and across to the Americas.
questions.more: It follows the edges of the Pacific plate, where the ocean floor slides under the continents and melts. About 90 per cent of the world's earthquakes happen along it too. Indonesia has more active volcanoes than any other country, and Japan has around 110.

questions.q: What does a meteorologist mean by 'relative humidity' of 100 per cent?
o: The air holds all the water vapour it can at that temperature
questions.w: The air is saturated, so vapour starts to condense into dew, fog or cloud.
questions.more: Warm air can hold far more vapour than cold, which is why a humid summer night feels sticky and a winter house feels dry. The dew point, the temperature at which the air would hit 100 per cent, is a better guide to how muggy it feels; above 20 degrees Celsius it is oppressive. Sweat cools you only if it can evaporate.

questions.q: What is the name of the supercontinent that held all the Earth's land about 300 million years ago, before it broke apart?
questions.w: Pangaea, Greek for 'all earth', a name coined by Alfred Wegener in 1915.
questions.more: Wegener was ridiculed for proposing that continents drift; he died on the Greenland ice cap in 1930 long before plate tectonics proved him right in the 1960s. Gondwana and Laurasia were the two halves Pangaea split into. The Atlantic is still widening by about two and a half centimetres a year, roughly the rate fingernails grow.

questions.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, which way do hurricanes spin?
o: It depends on the time of year
questions.w: Anticlockwise, because of the Coriolis effect of the Earth's rotation. In the Southern Hemisphere they spin clockwise.
questions.more: The same effect is why storms almost never form within five degrees of the equator, where there is no spin to get them going; a hurricane cannot cross the equator. The idea that bathwater drains the opposite way in Australia is a myth: the Coriolis force is far too weak at that scale, and the shape of the basin decides.

questions.q: The 1815 eruption of which volcano, the largest in recorded history, caused the 'year without a summer' and crop failures across Europe and North America?
questions.w: Tambora, on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, which blew off the top 1,400 metres of the mountain.
questions.more: Its ash dimmed the Sun worldwide; snow fell in New England in June 1816 and famine followed in Europe. Mary Shelley, kept indoors by the dreadful weather at Lake Geneva that summer, wrote Frankenstein. The disaster also prompted Karl Drais to invent an early bicycle, because so many horses had been eaten.
